preCheck.intro: Four quick questions before your first shift. They are not graded. They show you and your teacher where you are starting.

items.prompt: Which of these is an OBSERVATION about an object, not an inference?

options.text: The handle is worn smooth because it was used every day.
options.why: "Because it was used every day" is an explanation. It goes beyond what you can see.

options.text: The handle is smoother and paler than the rest of the wood.
options.why: Yes. This describes what anyone looking would see, without explaining it.

options.text: The object belonged to a carpenter.
options.why: This is a conclusion about the owner. It would need evidence.

items.prompt: A label card says an object is "the very first one ever made." What should you ask FIRST?

options.text: Who wrote this card, when, and how did they know?
options.why: Yes. That is sourcing: before you believe a document, ask who made it, when and why.
Looking old cannot show that something was the first of its kind.

options.text: Nothing. Museum labels are always checked.
options.why: Drafts, donor cards and old labels can be wrong. Checking them is part of the job.

items.prompt: Two sources disagree about when an object was made. What is the best next step?

options.text: Pick the one that sounds more confident.
Look for more evidence and compare how reliable each source is.
options.why: Yes. That is corroboration: compare sources and weigh their reliability.
Averaging does not make either source more accurate.

items.prompt: Which label sentence states uncertainty honestly?

options.text: This key definitely sent the first telegraph message.
options.why: "Definitely" claims more than the evidence supports.

options.text: This key is believed to come from the first Baltimore–Washington line, but we cannot say whether it sent the first message.
options.why: Yes. It says what the record supports and marks what remains unknown.

options.text: Nobody knows anything about this key.
options.why: That throws away what the evidence does show.

transfer.intro: Last task, on your own: a new object with no hints. A visitor's comment card (fictional) makes three claims about this Smithsonian scan. Use the photos and the record excerpt to decide.

card.title: Visitor comment card (fictional document created for this game)
card.body: "I think this compass was made by Western Electric in the 1830s, and it was donated by the inventor's family."

recordExcerpt: Date made: ca 1870. Maker: Western Electric
Physical description: rubber, glass, brass, copper, steel (part materials)
Credit line: from Western Union Corporation
Measurements: overall: 8 1/2 in x 7 1/2 in x 8 in; 21.59 cm x 19.05 cm x 20.32 cm

statements.text: A thin pointer sits over a pale round dial inside a horizontal ring.
The instrument was used to measure electric current.
statements.why: This is about purpose. The record names it a galvanometer but the photos alone cannot show its use.

statements.text: The tall hoop is made of copper.
statements.why: The record lists copper among its materials, but which part is copper cannot be seen in a photo.

claims.text: It was made by Western Electric.
claims.why: The record lists the maker as Western Electric.
The record dates it to about 1870.

claims.text: It was donated by the inventor's family.
claims.why: The credit line says it came "from Western Union Corporation", a company, not a family. (Who invented this design is not in the record.)

transfer.labelPrompt: Write one sentence for a public label about this object that states what is known and how sure we are.
transfer.exemplar: Tangent galvanometer made by Western Electric around 1870, which came to the Smithsonian from Western Union Corporation.
